evidence.title: Novice early-stage cyber uplift does not establish end-to-end attack gains
evidence.observation: Source-reported finding: RAND reports stronger early-stage novice uplift than end-to-end uplift in a randomized AI-access study. Complete-chain differences were generally statistically insignificant, and most participants failed harder chains with or without AI. Observation period and measurement context: September 2025–January 2026; randomized AI access for 157 participants and three CTF chains.
evidence.evidence_standing: Source-reported bounded account; study or measurement; not independently reproduced
evidence.glossary_fit: Illustrative or qualifying; does not validate a definition

source_locations.SRC-137: Executive summary, §§3.3–3.5, printed pp. 27–30 and methods context

evidence.limitations: Small sample, eight-hour sessions, timeout gates, simplified targets without active defense, possible control access to AI search, optional model use and then-current models. Insignificance does not establish no effect.
evidence.open_questions: Transfer to other populations, tasks and operating environments remains unestablished. Missing measurement details are not inferred.
evidence.support_assessment: Commons interpretation: Easier entry does not establish scalable end-to-end attack capability or autonomous goals.
evidence.dispute_status: See source version and dispute qualifications; no systematic clearance claimed.
evidence.verification_status: Not independently verified by the Commons

terms.name: Attacker-model change
terms.definition: A material shift in what adversaries can feasibly attempt, given available tools, knowledge, resources, speed, and scale. Exposure can increase even when the protected system and its controls remain unchanged.

terms.name: Capability feasibility progression
terms.definition: An analytical sequence for describing distinct levels of practical possibility: possible → practical → repeatable → scalable. A step need not follow the preceding one automatically, and the categories are not a universal maturity model.

relationships.explanation: Illustrates stage- and skill-dependent changes rather than a universal attacker uplift.
Qualifies extrapolation from early task success to practical end-to-end capability.
